scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The term 'ardah' is believed to derive from the Arabic verb 'ard', meaning 'to show' or 'to parade'.
Historically, the dance was performed by men of the Najd region to publicly demonstrate tribal combat strength and elevate morale before entering war.
In the 21st century, the Saudi government formally adopted the name 'Saudi Ardah' to distinguish this specific Najdi variant.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Alardah Alnajdiyah marks important personal, local, and national occasions, including weddings, births, and graduations.
It is a symbol of group cohesion and respect, serving as a vital expression of Saudi cultural identity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by two rows of men facing each other.
Participants move their bodies forward and backward in rhythm with the drums and poetry.
Dancers may brandish a sword or cane, raising and lowering it while tilting their hand to one side.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While Najdi Ardah is the most common and televised form in Saudi Arabia, other variations exist throughout the Arabian Peninsula.
The dance is part of the broader tradition of Ardah found across the Arabian Peninsula, sharing thematic similarities with other regional performances like the Mizmar and Yowlah.
